title: Java Packages
learningObjectives: Explain that packages group related Java types.
Distinguish built-in packages from user-defined packages.
Use import statements to refer to types by simple name.
Explain how package organization supports naming and access boundaries.

understand.concept: A package is a namespace that groups related classes and interfaces. Java provides built-in packages such as java.util and java.time. Developers can create their own packages using package declarations and organize source files to match package names.
understand.whyItMatters: Packages organize code, reduce naming conflicts and help define access boundaries. Imports make commonly used types easier to refer to without repeatedly writing their full names.
understand.analogy: Think of a well-designed object as a small service with a clear responsibility: it keeps the information it owns and exposes only the operations other code needs.
understand.analogyLimit: This analogy is only a design aid; Java access, inheritance and dispatch follow the language's exact rules.

explain.narrative:
## Built-in packages

Java's standard library groups types into packages. For example, `java.util` contains collections and utility classes, while `java.time` contains date and time types.

## Import types

An import statement lets source code refer to a type by its simple name. A fully qualified name includes the package, such as `java.util.ArrayList`. Importing does not copy the class into your project.

## User-defined packages

A source file can begin with a package declaration. Directory layout commonly mirrors the package name, and compilation tools place class files into corresponding output directories.

## Common mistakes

- Writing an import after a class declaration.
- Assuming importing a package automatically imports all nested packages.
- Confusing a package name with a class name.

examples.title: Use a type from java.util
examples.code:
import java.util.ArrayList;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<>(); names.add("Asha"); System.out.println(names.get(0)); } }
examples.explanation: The import allows ArrayList to be referenced by its simple name.

examples.title: Use a fully qualified class name
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { java.util.Scanner scanner = new java.util.Scanner("42"); System.out.println(scanner.nextInt()); scanner.close(); } }
examples.explanation: A fully qualified name identifies a type without an import statement.

examples.title: Import a date type
examples.code:
import java.time.LocalDate;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { LocalDate date = LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 5); System.out.println(date.getYear()); } }
examples.explanation: LocalDate belongs to the java.time package.

examples.title: Import utility sorting
examples.code:
import java.util.Arrays;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { int[] values = {4, 1, 3}; Arrays.sort(values); System.out.println(Arrays.toString(values)); } }
examples.explanation: Arrays is a utility class in java.util.

examples.title: Use two standard packages
examples.explanation: A source file can import types from multiple packages.
